extracted.intended_audience: academic journal editors, referees, and authors (ecology/academic peer review)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journal editors (and reviewers/authors) on how to respond when peer reviewers disagree about a manuscript, including decision strategies (reject, request another review, or take sides) and reviewer behaviors that reduce ambiguous disagreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject unless unanimous approval
rubrics_metrics.description: One common approach, especially at selective journals, is to reject the paper if anything less than unanimous or near-unanimous approval is received from referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is the path of least resistance and is usually justified because there are many good papers available and editors must make decisions somehow. It is also sometimes adopted because editors may not be specialists in the paper's topic and feel safest letting specialists' disagreement imply rejection (with the view that the manuscript can be published elsewhere if that decision is wrong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor decides who is right and explains reasoning to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor's job goes beyond choosing referees: when referees disagree on an important point or on their overall view, the editor should decide which reviewer is correct and communicate that decision and the reasoning to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions should be informed by the reviews but not dictated by them; simply telling authors to 'address the concerns of the referees' is not clear when referees conflict. Editors should give explicit guidance about how the manuscript can be improved based on their judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear direction for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should give authors clear, specific direction about how the manuscript could be improved rather than vague instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewers disagree, generic instructions ('address concerns') are unhelpful. Editors should identify which criticisms must be addressed and why, and ideally explain how the author can resolve conflicts between reviewers' comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain a third 'tiebreaker' review when genuinely unsure
rubrics_metrics.description: If two referees disagree, an editor can solicit a third reviewer to help resolve a substantive disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good reason to seek a tiebreaker is genuine uncertainty about how to resolve a substantive dispute between specialists. This is distinct from seeking a tiebreaker purely to cast a deciding vote on acceptance versus rejection, which the author regards as an abdication of editorial responsibility. The author notes this practice is likely rare in ecology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject with option to resubmit as a 'new' manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor may reject a paper when referees disagree but allow the authors to resubmit it as a new manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a hedging strategy: it removes the paper from the journal's immediate pipeline while giving authors a path to try again. The post notes this approach has been discussed previously and is used by some editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish implicit from substantive disagreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reviewers should recognize implicit disagreements (where one referee notes a problem and another does not mention it) versus genuine disagreements about whether something is problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit disagreements can arise because referees have different interests or because one spotted something the other missed; these are not true disagreements. Awareness of this distinction helps editors interpret reviews and decide whether further clarification or action is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers should explicitly state where there aren't problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing, explicitly note not only problems but also aspects of the manuscript you believe are fine, especially where you anticipate other referees might object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reviewer anticipates objections that other referees might raise, explaining why those objections are not a problem gives the author 'ammunition' against contrary reviewers and reduces the ambiguity editors face when resolving conflicting reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors may (appropriately) overrule negative reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors vary in willingness to take sides; it is acceptable for an editor to overrule a negative review if, after examining the disagreement, the editor judges the criticism unfounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When overruling a negative review, the editor should explain their reasoning to the author. Taking this responsibility is contrasted with simply tallying referee votes or outsourcing the decision to another tiebreaker reviewer merely to avoid taking a stand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial willingness to dig into details matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors differ in how much they are willing to investigate explicit or implicit disagreements among referees; greater willingness can lead to more constructive, directed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a continuum: some editors will only aggregate votes, while others will analyze the substance of disagreements and make a judgment. The post argues that digging into disagreements and providing a clear editorial stance benefits authors and the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using tiebreakers solely as a voting mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeking an extra review merely to get a tiebreaking vote on acceptance is inappropriate because it shifts editorial responsibility onto reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes using a tiebreaker for voting as an 'abdication of editorial responsibility' and hopes editors avoid this practice; a tiebreaker should be sought for substantive input when the editor is genuinely uncertain.
